newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling holds vs dlr after intervention.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling holds vs dlr after intervention.

text.p: The Kenyan shilling held steady against the dollar on Tuesday after the central bank sold dollars to commercial banks to enable nervous offshore investors to get out of the market on Monday, foreign exchange dealers said.
Commercial bank dealers said the central bank sold up to $21 million to meet orders from foreign investors who wanted to disinvest from government treasury bills.
"The market is stable now. Small flows -- but nothing significant," a senior dealer from a leading bank told Reuters.
Dealers said the shilling was trading around the 62.50/63.50 levels, unchanged from the closing rates on Monday.

The decision by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to cancel a key aid package to Kenya in a row over corruption last week rocked the foreign exchange market and sent the shilling plummeting to levels as low as 64.50.
It rebounded to 61.50 on Friday but the shilling suffered further losses on Monday, sliding to 63.50, a 3.35 percent drop on heavy dollar demand from nervous foreign investors.
The shilling weakened by a total of 6.72 percent from Thursday's close until Monday's close.
"There is still pressure on the shilling because as you can see the rates are not going down. If there was no pressure, rates would have gone down," a dealer said.
Some dealers said the bank's intervention helped calm the market by showing it was prepared and able to meet foreign demand for dollars when the need arose.
"It was good the central bank came in. Otherwise the shilling would have collapsed," a dealer told Reuters.
Some dealers said the market had settled to a nervous calm.
"The market is calm but it can be scattered anytime. The best position right now is to be long on dollars," one said.
Meanwhile inflows from coffee exporters trickled in on Tuesday but they were not seen as sufficient for the market.
"We have an offer of $231,000 from coffee but that's not enough to help out the market," another dealer told Reuters.
Last week Kenyan Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said that the government would let market forces determine shilling direction but it still hoped to maintain price stability.
In his first comment on the IMF ruling, President Daniel arap Moi said on Sunday that "the stoppage of financial aid to Kenya by the IMF was purely political and has no economic rationality".

The Kenyan cabinet on Monday appeared to rule out a quick return to negotiations with the International Monetary Fund, saying that Kenyans must depend on themselves to develop their country. But the cabinet also asked for investors' calm.

President Daniel arap Moi, aged 73 and in power since 1978, faces elections this year pitting the KANU party against an opposition that has found fragile cohesion in a campaign for constitutional reform. No election date has been set.
